notes.claim: A vector has both a magnitude and a direction, and velocity, force and acceleration are physical quantities it can represent.
Vector quantities cannot be added, subtracted, multiplied or divided by simply adding, subtracting, multiplying or dividing their magnitudes.
A vector is a quantity with a magnitude (length) and a direction, such as velocity, force or acceleration.
Two vectors with the same magnitude and direction are equal wherever they sit, so an arrow can be moved without changing the vector.
Moving backwards along a vector makes it negative, which means reversing its direction.
Vector components are the separate x, y and z values of a vector, and they can be added or subtracted separately.
A resultant vector is the vector that results from adding two or more vectors together.
Vectors cannot be added by adding their magnitudes, so combining two forces needs their directions as well.
The equilibrant has the same magnitude as the resultant but the opposite direction, so it balances the forces.
Components can be added separately, which gives the resultant part by part.
Subtracting a vector is the same as adding its negative version, and making a vector negative means reversing its direction.
Displacement is found by subtracting the initial position from the final position.
The velocity of object A relative to object B is the vector difference of their velocities, v_A minus v_B, in the same reference frame.
Marine engineers draw the vector diagrams for the inlet and outlet steam velocities over a moving turbine blade.
A common course-to-steer mistake is to 'join the dots', connecting the end of the tidal vector to the destination.
The scalar product of two vectors multiplies their magnitudes by the cosine of the angle between them and gives a number.
Work is defined as the scalar product of the force vector with the displacement vector.
The scalar product of orthogonal vectors is zero, and that of antiparallel vectors is negative.
The dot product is a scalar, whereas the cross product is a vector.
The apparent power of an AC circuit is the product of its RMS voltage and current, measured in volt-amperes (VA).
The size of the cross product multiplies the two magnitudes by the sine of the angle between them, and its direction follows the corkscrew right-hand rule.
For a right-hand rule, point the fingers along the first vector, curl them toward the second, and the thumb gives the direction of the cross product.
A wrench gives its best turning effect when the force is applied perpendicular to the handle.
The cross product is a vector, unlike the dot product, which is a scalar.
A current-carrying wire in a magnetic field feels a force perpendicular to both the current and the field.
The force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field is IlB sin θ, with its direction given by a right-hand rule.
Phasor voltages and currents can be added graphically exactly as vectors are.
A phasor is a complex number that represents the magnitude and phase of a voltage or current, and the dot product of phasors does not give another phasor.
Phasors can be divided but vectors cannot, according to one community answer (a secondary source).
Sinusoids of different frequencies cannot be drawn on the same phasor diagram because the phase angle between them changes with time.
